title: Make the ubuntu and macos jobs green again, and keep them read
acceptance: A run of the `ci` workflow on this branch has all five jobs green — `rust (windows-latest)`, `rust (ubuntu-latest)`, `rust (macos-latest)`, `shellcheck-secondary` and `bootstrap-validate-windows` — and the run id is named in the hand-back so the claim can be checked rather than believed.
On ubuntu and macos the test step actually executes: the log for each contains `test result:` lines and a passed count, rather than the job ending at clippy. The counts are reported per platform.

Every test that fails on a platform is either fixed or shown to be asserting that platform’s own path semantics, and in the second case it is gated to that platform with a comment saying why — the choice is made per test with the reason written down, not by disabling a suite.

The classification question is answered rather than assumed: `candidate_context::classify_path` and `recording_projection` decide by walking `path.components()`, so a Windows-style path given to them on Unix is one component and classifies differently from the same path on Windows, while `hook_protection`’s `folded` normalises `\` to `/` on every platform on purpose. Whether a path that arrives from outside the process must be normalised is stated in the code where it is decided, together with the effect the current answer has on a verdict.

Whatever is fixed is fixed in the source and not in the workflow: no job is made to skip a test, continue on error, or run a narrower command than it ran before, unless the hand-back says exactly which line changed and why that is not a way of not looking.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from a check of the branch's own CI runs, and placed first in the array so §14 dispatches it next. The `ci` workflow has failed on 75 consecutive runs. The last green run is 35193436468 (commit 6d69c51b, 2026-09-17T07:13Z); the first red is 35196110213 (commit 717fc0ad, 2026-09-17T07:45Z). The run table in progress/HANDOFF.md stops at 35174114907, which is before the last green run, so none of the streak is recorded anywhere and the loop has been treating five green Windows gates as the whole story. Three distinct causes were seen: (1) `cargo test` failing on `rust (windows-latest)` in 35196110213, where three tests in `crates/sure-core/tests/browser_driver.rs` (:367 `a_page_that_never_arrives_is_a_failure_of_the_project_and_not_an_absence`, :474 `a_healthy_local_page_is_opened_and_comes_back_green`, :550 `a_page_that_throws_and_asks_for_something_missing_reports_all_of_it`) panicked with `a browser was found at C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe and could not be driven: Absence { reason: DriverWouldNotStart, detail: "...ran for 19.999018 seconds without reporting a debugging port" }` — that message is the product's own false-green discipline working correctly, and the job is green today, so this cause is environmental or intermittent and must be characterised rather than assumed fixed; (2) `cargo test` failing on `rust (ubuntu-latest)`, with `candidate_context::tests::windows_separators_work` (panicking at crates/sure-core/src/candidate_context.rs:134) and `recording_projection::tests::file_write_event_is_projected` (panicking at crates/sure-core/src/recording_projection.rs:734) — both are the same root cause, and it is not merely a test problem: `classify_path` (candidate_context.rs:36-60) decides by iterating `path.components()`, so `tests\\foo.rs` is two components on Windows and one on Unix and classifies as Test there and Product here, and the projection's `basename` would be `src\\main.rs` on Unix rather than `main.rs`; title: Make the non-Windows configuration checkable from Windows
acceptance: A single documented command runs on this Windows machine, needs no administrator rights and no WSL, and fails when the non-Windows `cfg` set would fail to compile or would trip lints — the class that produced 75 red CI runs without ever being reproducible locally.

The command is demonstrated against the real defect rather than asserted to work: a `#[cfg(windows)]`-only helper is reintroduced ungated, the command is run and shown to fail by naming it, and the helper is removed again. Both outputs are quoted in the hand-back.

Its cost is measured and stated as a wall-clock figure, because a check nobody can afford to run is a check nobody runs, and the figure decides whether it belongs in the local gate set listed in CLAUDE.md or in a slower pre-push path.

Whatever it needs installed is written down with the install command, and the check reports what is missing rather than failing obscurely when it is absent — a developer who cannot run it should be told to install a target, not left to decode a linker error.

If no such command can be made to work from native Windows, that is a valid outcome only with the attempts recorded and the reason spelled out: what was tried, what it did, and what a developer on Windows is then supposed to do instead. "It did not work" without the attempts is not an answer.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from the investigation of the 75-run CI failure streak recorded at item 99 of progress/HANDOFF.md. The streak's three significant defects — `candidate_context::tests::windows_separators_work` and `recording_projection::tests::file_write_event_is_projected` failing on Unix, `recheck_lifecycle::tests::keys_match_case_insensitively_on_windows` failing on its own Unix branch, and three helpers in `crates/sure-testkit/tests/integration_thinness.rs` that are live only on Windows and so are dead code under `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` — share one property: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` on Windows compiles the Windows cfg set, in which those helpers are used, so the failures are unreproducible on the only machine this loop develops on. The class is caught, by design, on ubuntu and macos — but only there, and only if someone reads the run. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` pins toolchain 1.98.1 and runs fmt, check, clippy, test on a three-OS matrix; nothing in the repository passes `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` or `--target x86_64-apple-darwin`, there is no pre-push hook, and there is no local substitute. So the blind spot is structural rather than a missed step, and the fix is a local command rather than more discipline. Candidates to evaluate rather than assume: `rustup target add` plus `cargo check --target <triple>` or `cargo clippy --target <triple>`, which needs no linker for check-only work; a `cfg`-auditing pass over the source; or building the Windows cfg set with the non-Windows arms forced, which is cheaper but less faithful. Constraint from CLAUDE.md: this must work natively on Windows and must not require moving anything into WSL, so a WSL-only answer does not satisfy the task. Note the asymmetry that made this class invisible for so long and that the acceptance is designed around: the same commit added four helpers, three ungated Windows-only and one used from an ungated test, and only the three produced errors. Measured on 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while verifying P15-T016, which narrows this task from "is it possible" to "how far does it reach". `rustup target list --installed` on this Windows machine already lists `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` and `x86_64-apple-darwin`, and `cargo clippy -p sure-testkit --all-targets --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -- -D warnings` exits 0 (in 0.15 s, cached; P15-T016's worker ran it uncached and used a deliberate `#[cfg(not(windows))]` dead-code probe to confirm the command really compiles that file for Linux rather than doing nothing). The same target does NOT reach the crates that link SQLite: `cargo check -p sure-core --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` exits 101 inside `cc-rs` with `error occurred in cc-rs: failed to find tool "x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc": program not found`, because the bundled `libsqlite3-sys` needs a cross C compiler this machine does not have. title: Tell a person when a recorded allowance cannot be spent
acceptance: Recording an allowance in a project whose settings make every matching request unanswerable by that allowance does not end in a plain success: the command either refuses and says why, or records and says what will actually happen — observed by running it in such a project and reading what it writes, not by reading the code.

The reason is stated in the user’s terms and names the setting that causes it, so a person can change that setting or stop expecting the allowance to work; it does not name the internal mode value alone.

The confirmation a user reads when an allowance *can* be spent no longer promises an outcome the settings make unreachable, and the confirmation for one that cannot is a different sentence rather than the same sentence plus a caveat.

Whatever is chosen, the store is left consistent with it: an allowance that is refused is not written, and one that is written is one a matching request can actually spend. Proved by reading the store back after both cases.
The command still records an allowance for every project where one can be spent, so the fix does not narrow what P13-T005 delivered.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from P13-T005's verification. Driven through target/debug/sure.exe against a scratch project outside the repository, with the payload the supervisor wrote: a project whose sure.yaml says `execution: mode: inspect_only`, then `hook allow-once --project <that project> --tool Shell --command "rm -rf build/"` exits 0 and prints "SURE recorded a one-time allowance for tool 'Shell', for the request 'rm -rf build/'." followed by "SURE would then let that one request through, if SURE names it as deleting a whole location, overwriting published commits, or reading a file of credentials." The request it was recorded for is then still blocked, unchanged, with "The current execution mode does not permit this action." — and it stays blocked however many times it is sent. The cause is not a bug in the spend path: under a mode that does not run project code, `consent::decide_for` answers an arbitrary command `Denied` rather than `NeedsConsent` (`crates/sure-core/src/consent.rs:491-501`, because `CommandClass::Destructive.required_permission()` is `None` at `crates/sure-domain/src/execution.rs:631`), and `hook_protection::assess_request` reads a danger only for `NeedsConsent` (`crates/sure-core/src/hook_protection.rs:426-429`), so no danger is ever named and `with_any_allowance` returns at its first line (`crates/sure-cli/src/hook.rs:416-418`). That refusal is deliberate and correct — `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md` states that a request held for any other reason cannot be let through by an allowance, and "an allowance is not a way to run under settings the user did not change". What is wrong is only what the user is told at the moment they record the grant: the command has `--project`, could read the mode, and instead reports a success and a promise that this project's settings make unreachable. The safe direction holds throughout — nothing dangerous is allowed — so this is a false reassurance and a silent no-op, not a false green. Related but distinct: `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md` says the *subject* is deliberately not checked at write time, because there is no request to read then, and a grant no request ever matches is spent by nothing and expires; that stays as it is and this task does not ask for it. The mode, unlike the subject, is knowable at write time.

title: Decide what a change to the project's files is, because no setting can allow one
acceptance: The question is answered rather than left implicit: either a configuration this build ships can grant permission to change the project's files, or none can and every surface says so. Observed by running the hook under a configuration the answer names and reading what the sentence and the store say, not by reading the vocabulary.

What the product says and what it does are the same thing. `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md` describes a change as held when it lands in a migration, CI/CD config, a secret or config area, or names a whole location rather than a file — which promises that a change nowhere near those is not held. If in fact every change is refused in every mode, the document is corrected to say so; if not, the mode holds what it says it holds. Observed by driving one ordinary change and one sensitive change through the hook and reading both answers.

The two allowance sentences agree with whatever is decided. `sure hook allow-once` for a tool whose only action is a change (`Write`, `Delete`, and `Edit` after `P13-T010`) refuses or records with a reason that is true and names no setting that is not the cause, and no sentence in the product says a change is held only sometimes where the decision path holds it always.

The answer is one rule and not two. The decision path (`sure_domain::execution::decide`), the protection mode's own question, and the reachable-act computation the allowance writer reads are asked the same question and give the same answer, proved by a test that fails when one of them moves without the others.
Whatever a change is allowed to do, it is observed at the process boundary for both harnesses with the store read back, so the answer is a fact about a run and not about a reading of the tables.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while accepting P13-T010, from a gap that task's second send-back measured and deliberately did not fix (its brief says so in as many words: adding a `ProjectRequest::WriteProject` variant is a configuration-vocabulary change outside that task). WHAT WAS MEASURED, ON `e270fe8`, WITH THE BINARY THAT TIP BUILDS: (1) `crates/sure-domain/src/execution.rs`'s `required_permission` maps `ActionKind::WriteProjectFile | ActionKind::DeleteProjectFile` to `Permission::WriteProject`, and `decide` returns `Denied` whenever `permissions.allows(required)` is false — before the mode and before any protection question. (2) Nothing in this build sets `write_project` true: `ProjectRequest` has seven variants (`RunProjectCode`, `InstallDependencies`, `Network`, `FullRecording`, `Telemetry`, `ExternalAnalysis`, `ExtendedRetention`) and no arm of `ProjectRequest::permission()` returns `WriteProject`; `Authority::permissions()` (`crates/sure-core/src/config/authority.rs`) starts from `ExecutionPermissions::inspect_only()` and sets a permission only from a *granted* privilege's `request.permission()`; and the only `write_project: true` in the tree is inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module (`crates/sure-core/src/core_flow.rs:987`, module opens at line 631). So `decide` denies a file change in every mode, under every configuration a user can build. (3) Driven at the process boundary: with the user's own settings file naming `execution.mode: host_confirmed` (so `run_project_code` is granted), a Claude Code `PreToolUse` event naming `Edit` for `src/lib.rs` is answered **Block**, "The current execution mode does not permit this action." — so a harness's ordinary file edit is refused in a configuration that explicitly allowed project code to run. THE DOCUMENT DISAGREES. `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md` line 39 and its neighbours describe a change as held when it 'lands in a migration, CI/CD config, secret/config areas' or 'names a whole location rather than a file', which is a description of a mode that lets ordinary changes through. The code refuses all of them. One of the two is wrong and the task is to find out which. NOT A DUPLICATE OF: `P13-T010` (accepted after this task was minted, and about the *sentence* an allowance refusal is answered with — this is about whether the permission can be granted at all, which is the fact that sentence has to describe); `P13-T004` and `P13-T005` (the protection modes and the one-time allowance); `P15-T022` ('Let a person make the grants that only their own file can make', which is about `full_recording` and `execution.mode` and names no write permission); `P15-T025` ('Let a caller name the settings file', which is the flag that would let this question be driven from the command line rather than from a test — a convenience for this task's evidence, not its subject). NOT MEASURED HERE, AND THE FIRST THING THE TASK SHOULD SETTLE: whether refusing every change is the intended posture — SURE is a checking layer and not a coding-agent orchestrator, so 'the hook never authorises an agent to write' is a defensible product position rather than an oversight. If it is intended, the acceptance is that every surface says so plainly and the document stops promising otherwise; if it is not, the acceptance is a permission the user's own file can grant. The hand-back states which it found and what the evidence for it is.

ACCEPTED 2026-09-20 at 8342764. The acceptance sentence — "aarch64 macOS artifact builds/tests and checksum generated in CI/release environment" — is met by CI run 35512934506 (`release-dry-run`, workflow_dispatch), all four jobs success, with the artifact uploaded as `sure-aarch64-apple-darwin` (4054412 bytes).

WHAT WAS BUILT. `scripts/Build-Release.sh` (new in this task's first commit c522699, corrected in 8342764; 1307 -> 1341 lines) packages the aarch64-apple-darwin build into a tar.gz beside a `sha256sum`-format .sha256, extracts it to a fresh scratch directory and runs the extracted binary from there, so the property it establishes is the one the Windows script already states: the bytes that are checksummed are the bytes that were run. The architecture is read from the binary's own first eight bytes and required to be `cffaedfe0c000001` — 64-bit Mach-O, little-endian, CPU_TYPE_ARM64 — rather than believed from the runner's label, and `/usr/bin/file` is asked the same question as a second, independent reader. `--phase all` builds, packages, checksums and checks; `--phase verify` re-checks an archive without building, so a downloaded artifact can be judged without a toolchain.

THE ARCHITECTURE READING, which is the point of the task. The macOS job printed `header cffaedfe0c000001`, `reads as Mach-O 64-bit, arm64`, `file says Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64`, and the RESULT block's `arch  Mach-O 64-bit, arm64, read from the header bytes cffaedfe0c000001`. Two readers, one of them the kernel's own loader format, agreeing on the shipped bytes rather than on the file name or the runner image label. The artifact: `sure-0.0.0-bootstrap-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz`, 4065656 bytes, sha256 3308bb2c12aee7008ed7734565775e96cc092a6c46c1b2efaea87e6d2c820c23, "computed by sha256sum" and re-read from disk; layout "4 entries, exactly the promised set". This could not have been produced on the development host, where no aarch64 std and no aarch64 C toolchain exist (rustc E0463; cc-rs `failed to find tool "cc"`), which is why the task names the CI environment.

THE TWO RED RUNS THIS TASK PRODUCED, AND WHAT THEY WERE. `ci` 35510588761 was red at `shellcheck-secondary`: SC2006/SC2034 at Build-Release.sh:881 and SC2006 at :965. Both were real defects and not lint noise. At :881 an unquoted heredoc delimiter meant backticks in the body were command substitution, so the shipped RELEASE.txt lost the twelve characters of `Signature=adhoc` — and the substitution ran. At :965 backticks inside a double-quoted `fail` string actually executed `sha256sum -c` and swallowed the failure message the check existed to print. The macOS artifact job failed after every substantive step had already passed, on the `running from` comparison; and `validate (ubuntu-latest)` failed for a reason that predates this task, proved by the commit's own hunk arithmetic — the validate job's steps are context lines (old 6-18 = new 19-31), so the job was already broken and this commit merely re-ran it.

(2) The double-quoted backticks at :965 executing `sha256sum -c` and corrupting the failure message. INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED BY THE SUPERVISOR, from the shipped bytes rather than from the hand-back: the four committed files' digests and line counts; `sh -n scripts/Build-Release.sh` exit 0; the workflow YAML parsed, with the AppArmor step present and conditioned on ubuntu and placed before the test step; the corrected comparison block lifted out of the shipped file by `sed` and driven with planted inputs, where the OLD block given the runner's own two paths reproduces run 35510588722's failure exactly and the NEW block passes it while still failing a different directory and a sibling name (`sure.old`) — five cases, both directions; the shipped RELEASE.txt heredoc rendered by hand, printing `` `Signature=adhoc` that is what it is. `` with the `$(date -u ...)`, `$(uname -s)` and `$(uname -m)` expansions intact; the corrected `fail` message rendering whole with stderr empty and no `sha256sum` process spawned; a backtick sweep of the whole script finding exactly three non-comment backtick lines, all three escaped; and the manifest regeneration changing exactly three digests and no paths, each new digest re-hashed against the file it names.

acceptance: No sequence of suite runs exhausts any copy of the helper: after the pool that exists today has been deliberately filled, a fresh run still gets a directory rather than panicking, observed by filling it and running the suite rather than by reading the allocator.

All nineteen copies are addressed, not the one the title names. The count is established by a case-sensitive search for the shared shape — `create_dir` with `Err(error) if error.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists => continue` inside a `for _ in 0..1_000` loop — and by a search covering every wording of the exhaustion panic (`no free store directory under`, `no free directory under`, `no free fixture name under`, `no free control name under`, `no free scratch name under`), and the fix states how the count was taken. The nineteen sites map to twenty-two `target/tmp` pools, because one allocator is parameterised over four base names, and the count of pools — like the count of sites — is established by a search rather than restated from this criterion. Measured at P13-T004's acceptance: all 1,000 of store-0 .. store-999 existed — 1,340 directories, every one named store-N or project-N, no files — so the_protection_mode_a_project_names_is_the_one_sure_decides_under failed when run alone and would have failed in a full run. The accepted gate run at 1454c8e was green and consumed the last headroom; one full suite run allocates about 123 names, so it recurs after roughly eight runs. The supervisor cleared the scratch subtree and the gates re-ran green, which buys about eight runs and fixes nothing. This is the verification instrument, not the product: the failure is loud and on a correct tree, and the damage it does is to make a worker doubt its own change or edit product code around it. It belongs beside P15-T010 (cross-platform CI matrix) and P16-T003 (final cross-platform core gates), both of which need the suite to run repeatedly on one machine. MEASURED AGAIN AT P13-T009'S ACCEPTANCE (2026-09-19), AND THIS TIME THE FAILURE WAS TOTAL RATHER THAN PARTIAL: the worker could not run `cargo test` at all until it deleted 3,641 directories under `target/tmp/sure cli contract` — its own words, "the helper's name counter is per-process and starts at 0, so once the first 1000 names were consumed every run of that file panicked". That is a worse outcome than the one recorded above: at P13-T004 one test failed and said so; here the file could not start. THE POOL AS THE SUPERVISOR MEASURED IT, after that deletion and roughly five suite runs: 920 directories, `store-0` … `store-795` (783 of them) and `project-0` … `project-726` (137). THE FIGURE ABOVE — "about eight runs", "buys about eight runs" — SHOULD NOT BE REUSED, and reading the allocator says why. `a_directory_of_our_own` tries at most 1,000 candidates in a loop whose counter is shared by every prefix and starts at 0 in each process, so what a call needs is not a free name anywhere but a free name for *its own prefix* within 1,000 attempts of wherever the counter stands; a fresh process's first call walks from 0 and therefore needs the first gap in that prefix's taken set, which is one past its highest index. The binding number is the highest index for the busiest prefix (795 today), not the total directory count, and it grows by roughly a whole run's allocation each time the suite runs. On this reading the pool is within about one full suite run of the panic, not eight, and the next session that runs the suite should read this paragraph before assuming it has headroom. Nothing was changed to fix it: this is the record, P15-T015 is the task.

MEASURED AGAIN ON 2026-09-20, AND THE ALLOCATOR HAS THREE MORE INSTANCES THAN THIS NOTE NAMED. THE FAILURE HAS MOVED TO A DIFFERENT POOL, AND IT IS NOW `cargo test` DYING RATHER THAN ONE TEST FAILING. Clearing `sure commands` buys roughly ninety suite runs at about eleven allocations per run, which is why the clean-up is worth doing and why it is not the fix.

ONE THING ABOUT THE ALLOCATOR IS UNEXPLAINED, AND IS RECORDED RATHER THAN EXPLAINED AWAY. `sure mcp protocol` passed all twenty-five of its tests with 2,289 contiguous directories present, twice, the second time after the test source was touched to force a rebuild — which the 1,000-attempt bound above says cannot happen. Deleting `store-500` from that pool showed the scan does start at zero, because the next run recreated `store-500` rather than a high name; and a later run was observed creating `store-2374`, an index no 1,000-iteration loop can reach. The source of that helper is byte-identical to the two that behave as documented. Whatever the resolution turns out to be, it does not make the pools safe: the observable defect is that the suite has already failed twice on this allocator and will fail again.

THE COUNT IN THE PARAGRAPH ABOVE IS WRONG, AND IT IS WRONG IN THE WAY THAT PARAGRAPH ITSELF DESCRIBES. It says the allocator is written four times: `cli_contract.rs`, `commands.rs`, `mcp_protocol.rs` and `mcp.rs`. The real number is NINETEEN, and the mistake was mine and is worth naming because a worker will repeat it. I found the extra instances by grepping for the panic sentence, and I grepped for ONE WORDING of it. The sentence has five: `no free store directory under` 3 times, `no free directory under` once, `no free fixture name under` 10 times, `no free control name under` 3 times, `no free scratch name under` twice. Grepping `no free (store )?directory under` therefore finds 4 of 19 and looks complete, which is a claim about the whole tree made from a sample of it — the exact defect the paragraph above was written to complain about.

The nineteen are established two independent ways and the two agree one-to-one, which is why the number can be written down. `create_dir` followed by `Err(error) if error.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists => continue` inside a `for _ in 0..1_000` loop occurs 19 times, across 19 files, one per file. The exhaustion `panic!("no free ...")` occurs 19 times too, in those same 19 files. Both counts were taken with a case-sensitive content search over `crates`, not from memory. The files are: `sure-cli/src/commands.rs`, `sure-cli/src/mcp.rs`, `sure-cli/src/check.rs`, `sure-cli/tests/mcp_protocol.rs`, `sure-cli/tests/cli_contract.rs`, `sure-core/src/components.rs`, `sure-core/src/discover/pattern.rs`, and twelve under `sure-core/tests/`: `config_references.rs`, `finding_severity_rule.rs`, `components_graph.rs`, `env_completeness.rs`, `document_commands.rs`, `benign_fixture_e2e.rs`, `adversarial_fixture_detection.rs`, `db_migrations.rs`, `dependency_state.rs`, `intent_sources.rs`, `support_levels.rs`, `setup_validation.rs`. Five of the nineteen are in `src/` rather than `tests/` — `sure-cli/src`'s `commands.rs`, `mcp.rs` and `check.rs`, and `sure-core/src`'s `components.rs` and `discover/pattern.rs` — but all five sit behind `#[cfg(test)]` inside a `mod tests`, so they are unit-test code and are NOT in the shipped binary. This paragraph originally said the opposite; the correction, and how the claim was checked the second time, is below. The other fourteen are test files.

A fix written against four files, or against the one file this task was minted for, would leave fifteen copies of the defect in place and would report success. If the five wordings are collapsed into one first, `grep` becomes a usable check for whether the copy is really gone.

THE ANOMALY IS NOW MEASURED RATHER THAN MERELY OBSERVED. The paragraph above records that `sure mcp protocol` passed with a pool the 1,000-attempt bound says should have blocked it. That was an observation; on 2026-09-20, during a six-gate run at `d819d57`, it became a measurement, and the measurement is what makes it a defect in the stated rule rather than a curiosity. Before the gate, `target/tmp/sure cli contract` held 4,062 `store-N` directories with `store-0` .. `store-999` all present, and `target/tmp/sure mcp protocol` held 2,375 with `store-0` .. `store-999` all present; a script over every pool under `target/tmp` confirmed `store-*` was the blocked prefix in both, and that no other prefix in either pool was blocked. After the gate the same two pools held 4,193 and 2,404 directories — up 131 and up 29. Directories appearing during the run is the allocator running; both suites passed every test. Nothing in either pool was touched by hand between the two readings, and the extraction was the only pool cleared.

So a call does find a free name in a pool whose first thousand names for that prefix are occupied, and the explanation above cannot account for it. What follows for whoever implements this task: do not derive the fix from the stated rule alone. The rule is a reading of the source and the source is right, but something outside the reading — the order prefixes are first asked for within a process, which helper a given test actually reaches, or a base path that differs from the one scanned — makes the behaviour differ from it, and nobody has established which. Prefer a fix whose correctness does not depend on being right about which prefix binds: bounding the total number of directories under a pool, or reusing one directory for the length of a run, is correct under either model.

THE PARAGRAPH ABOVE NAMED THE WRONG CONSEQUENCE, AND A CORRECTION TO IT IS PART OF THIS NOTE. It said the five `src/` copies "are reached by the shipped binary and not only by the suite, which makes this not a test-only concern". They are not, and it is not. Every one of the five sits after a `#[cfg(test)]` and inside a `mod tests`, so those five compile into their crates' unit-test targets and never into a shipped `sure` or `sure-cli`. Measured at `96c490b` by listing each file's `#[cfg(test)]` and `mod tests` line numbers and comparing them with the allocator's panic line: `sure-cli/src/mcp.rs` cfg `:1026`, allocator `:1064`; `commands.rs` cfg `:212`, allocator `:245`; `check.rs` cfg `:741`, allocator `:785`; `sure-core/src/components.rs` cfg `:750`, allocator `:781`; `discover/pattern.rs` cfg `:211` and `:254`, allocator `:274`. Every `cfg(test)` precedes its allocator. The sentence in the paragraph above has been replaced rather than left standing beside this one.

The claim was wrong because it was inferred rather than measured: "this file is under `src/`" was read as "this code ships", and one command would have shown otherwise. That is the same failure as the four-of-nineteen count corrected above, in the same note, made by the same person within the same hour. Both times the instrument was a reading of the tree taken from a sample rather than from the tree.

WHAT THE CORRECTION DOES NOT CHANGE IS THE SCOPE. The task is still all nineteen copies, and criterion 1 still asks that no sequence of suite runs exhaust any of them. The reason is simply not the one that was written: it is that **not one of the nineteen reclaims its pool**, so each is a fixed thousand-name budget that only a person clears. Whether the copy lives in `tests/` or behind `#[cfg(test)]` in `src/` makes no difference to that, and the failure that started this task — `sure commands` — was in one of the five. Nothing ships with the defect; everything running `cargo test` has it.

AND THE POOLS NUMBER TWENTY-TWO, NOT FIVE. The inventory paragraph above counts panic WORDINGS, and there are five of those, but the directories are more numerous because one allocator is parameterised. Eighteen allocators hardcode their base; the nineteenth, `crates/sure-core/tests/adversarial_fixture_detection.rs:255`, is `fn under(base_name: &str, test: &str)` and is called with four distinct base names — `adversarial python controls` (via `new()` at `:247`), `claim evidence fixtures` (`:1335`), `adversarial intent controls` (`:2964`) and `adversarial execution trust controls` (`:3523` and `:3754`). Eighteen plus four is twenty-two pools, each with its own `static NEXT` and its own `for _ in 0..1_000`, so the aggregate budget is twenty-two thousand names rather than five thousand. Verified at `96c490b` by reading the function and grepping its call sites.

THE POOLS ALREADY CARRY THE PATHS THE WINDOWS DISCIPLINE DEMANDS, AND A FIX MUST NOT REGRESS THEM. Measured on 2026-09-20 by reading the directory with a tool that does not split on whitespace: of the names under `target/tmp`, 52 contain whitespace and 25 contain non-ASCII characters — `sure 指纹 checks`, `sure 扫描 scan`, `a release directory with é中文 and spaces`. Every one of the twenty-two Family A pool names was found on disk verbatim, which is the same census taken from the other direction and is the cross-check that was missing when the count was four. The wider names are why the fix must not rebuild a path through anything that splits on spaces or assumes ASCII; `CLAUDE.md` already requires this ("Test paths with spaces, Unicode and long path pressure"), so a regression here would be caught by the names that already exist rather than by a test somebody has to think to write.

No count of `target/tmp` belongs in this note, and none is given. That directory is a live scratch area the suite writes to while a census is taken — two readings a few minutes apart during this work differed by hundreds of entries — so any total is a snapshot of a running process and not a property of the repository. The durable artifact is the set of names, and the population this task is about is defined by the design and not by a directory listing: the shape search is the instrument, and a listing is at best a cross-check on it.

Two traps sit beside that number, both met while establishing it. First, `target/tmp/doctor_contract` looks like a pool and is not one: `crates/sure-core/tests/doctor.rs:46-67` names its directory with the process id and calls `fs::remove_dir_all` on it first, treating `NotFound` as the ordinary case, so it reclaims and never matched the shape search. It is the nearest thing this repository has to a precedent for the fix, and its own header (`:33-45`) records that the concurrency mechanism it implements "was not confirmed" — read it before copying it. Second, a census taken by listing `target/tmp` is not a census at all: that directory is a live scratch area shared by several unrelated designs, so it holds far more than twenty-two entries and its contents change while the suite runs. The instrument that answers this task's question is the shape search, because the population is defined by the design and not by the directory.

title: Ask the volume, not the operating system, whether two paths are one file
acceptance: The claim is measured before anything is changed: on the macOS CI job, or any macOS machine this loop can drive, two spellings of one path (`src/EMAIL/SEND.rs` and `src/email/send.rs`) are put to the filesystem and what it answers is quoted with the command that asked. If on that machine they are two different files, this task's premise is wrong and its valid outcome is to be closed with that measurement recorded and no code changed around it — "the premise held" is not to be assumed from the platform's name.

The mechanism is chosen rather than assumed. `recheck_lifecycle::normalise_path` (`crates/sure-core/src/recheck_lifecycle.rs:57-67`) folds case under `#[cfg(windows)]` and is the question's whole answer today; it is compiled into `FindingKey::new`, so it decides whether a previous finding matches this run's finding. Case sensitivity belongs to the volume and not to the operating system — macOS ships case-insensitive volumes by default and can also hold case-sensitive ones, and a Linux mount can be either — so whatever replaces this must say at the decision what it is asking, what it does when it cannot tell, and which way it errs when it cannot tell.

The consequence is stated as a verdict-level effect and not only as a test: two spellings of one file must not become two findings for one issue, and a previous finding must not be carried open beside this run's copy of it. The hand-back says which of those the current code does, on which platform, measured rather than reasoned.

A test pins the behaviour on every platform. Any assertion that has to differ by platform says what it is asking that platform and why, in the pattern P15-T016 landed in `candidate_context` and `recheck_lifecycle`; a loosened or removed assertion is not an answer.

Anything that cannot be run on the machine this loop develops on is reported as not measured rather than inferred, and a check that a filesystem probe needs in order to be meaningful states what it does when the probe itself fails.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor, from P15-T016's hand-back and the supervisor's own reading of the code. The reading: `normalise_path` (`recheck_lifecycle.rs:57-67`) returns `trimmed.to_lowercase()` under `#[cfg(windows)]` and `trimmed.to_owned()` otherwise; it is called from `FindingKey::new` for both `location` and `locator`, so the key that decides whether a previous finding is the same finding is case-folded on Windows and case-preserving everywhere else — including the macOS jobs, whose `#[cfg(not(windows))]` branch is the one P15-T016's worker had to correct. The consequence P15-T016 measured on a case-sensitive filesystem: `keys_match_case_insensitively_on_windows` reports two findings for what Windows reports as one, and the previous finding is carried open beside the current one rather than matched. That is correct on Linux and is the open question on macOS, where the default volume is case-insensitive, so the same two spellings name one file and SURE reports it twice. Nothing about this is a false green — it is duplicate material and a missed match, not a pass — which is why it is a task with its own acceptance rather than a stop-the-line like P15-T016. It is deliberately not answered inside P15-T016: the fix moves what the product reports on a supported platform, and that is a decision with evidence of its own. Related but distinct: P4-T007's case-sensitivity work is about the check plan and the fixtures it added are what the Unix branch of that test exercises; this task is about the reconciler's identity question.

title: Make the program a test executes one that nothing is still writing
acceptance: Every fixture that copies a file and then executes it is found and listed, not only the ones already named. The record that prompts this task names two fixtures; `grep -rn "fs::copy" crates/*/tests/` finds four call sites, and the hand-back lists each with the command that found it and says for each whether the thing it copies is later executed. A fixture that copies a binary and runs it and is left off that list is a fixture left unfixed.

The mechanism is stated as the kernel's rule and not as a story about threads. `ETXTBSY` is raised at `execve` when the inode being executed is open for writing by *any* process; `fork` duplicates the descriptor table into the child, which is how a write descriptor held by one thread's `fs::copy` comes to be held by another thread's about-to-`execve` child; and `O_CLOEXEC` closes that descriptor at the child's own `execve`, which is the moment just after the window that matters. The hand-back says which of these the fix rests on, which it does not, and which of them it could not check from this machine.

The path that is executed is never a path with an open write descriptor. Whatever form the fix takes, the inode at the executed path must be complete and closed before anything can execute it — the proposal already recorded is to copy to a unique temporary name, close, and rename into place — and the hand-back says what window is left afterwards and why it is narrower, argued from the mechanism in the previous criterion rather than from the failure having become rarer.

The residual window is treated as a property of `fork` rather than as something a fix removes, and any retry is bounded, named and placed deliberately. If a retry is added, the hand-back says which error it retries and which errors it passes through unchanged, what the bound is, and where it lives. A retry in `sure-core`'s product code that exists so that a test can pass is not an answer: the product's job where it stands is to report what the operating system said, and in every recorded occurrence it did exactly that — `Error`, never a pass. A retry inside a fixture must not be able to turn a program that genuinely cannot be started into a pass.

What was reproduced is separated from what was reasoned. Windows has no `ETXTBSY`, so the platform that fails is not a platform this loop can run, and anything demonstrated instead — a test of the rule the fix rests on, a reading of the fixture that shows the executed path is closed, or a run of the suite under load — is reported as what it is. A criterion that cannot be met on this machine is reported as not met rather than inferred from the platform's name.

The verification is a number of runs and not the word "fixed". The falsifier already in `progress/HANDOFF.md` says a flake that has stopped appearing has not thereby been explained. The hand-back names how many executions of the `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` step of `rust (ubuntu-latest)` came back with zero failures, with their run ids, and states what would falsify the change. Until that number exists, the honest closing sentence is the one the existing section already ends on.

The record is corrected where it is wrong rather than only added to. The existing section and the P5-T003 run rows name two fixtures and say the failure rate is unknown; the hand-back corrects them in place — the number of call sites, the occurrences as they then stand, and whether the rate is still unknown — in the pattern the sections around them are kept in. A section left saying two when the tree has more is a correction the next reader will not get.

title: Give the checksum manifest a reader, or take it out of the tree
acceptance: The premise is measured and the measurement is in the hand-back, not asserted from this task's notes. Two things are shown with the command that showed them: that nothing in the repository reads `SHA256SUMS.txt` — no script, no workflow, no test, no Rust code, only prose about it — and that both of the bootstrap gates exit 0 over a manifest that is out of date. A hand-back that repeats this task's own sentence back is not a measurement.

The outcome is a decision that is stated as one. Keeping a file nothing reads is not neutral: it looks like assurance, and a reader who finds it will assume something checks it. The two honest outcomes are to give it a reader or to remove it and say what, if anything, took over its job. Either is acceptable and the hand-back argues for the one it chose; leaving it unread while saying nothing is not, because then its only function is to look like a check.

If it stays, what the check hashes is stated, and it is the same form the manifest was built from. `.gitattributes` sets `eol=crlf` for some paths, so the index blob and the checkout differ in length for those — measured on 2026-09-19: `scripts/install.ps1` is 2388 bytes in the index and 2426 bytes in the working tree, and a check that compares a working-tree digest against an index-derived manifest reports two mismatches that are not staleness. The hand-back says which of the two the check reads and why, and the answer is checked by running it against a manifest known to be correct.

If it gets a reader, that reader runs where a reader can fail. It joins the local gate set and a CI job, or the hand-back gives a written reason why not — and "the check would be red" is not a reason, because a check that is red because the manifest is stale is telling the truth about the tree. A check that runs only when someone remembers to run it is the situation this task exists to end, one level up.

The means of maintaining the file is in the repository, or the file is gone. `target/tmp/regen-sums.mjs` is currently the only thing that can regenerate it and `target/` is not committed, so no contributor has it — measured: `find . -name "regen-sums*" -not -path "./target/*"` returns nothing. Whatever the decision, the hand-back says where the regeneration lives after it, and a contributor on a fresh clone can follow that sentence to a file that exists.

The check does not make the commit rhythm impossible, and the hand-back says what a contributor must run before committing. The manifest hashes `progress/HANDOFF.md`, `progress/state.json` and `tasks/tasks.json`, so every acceptance commit changes three files it covers — measured: `grep -cE "^[0-9a-f]{64}  (progress|tasks)/" SHA256SUMS.txt` is 8, four under each. A check that is guaranteed red on the commit that records an acceptance is worse than no check, and the flow that satisfies it — stage, regenerate, commit — is either the one this loop already follows or the one the task replaces it with, stated plainly enough to be followed on the next task.

The self-reference is answered rather than left to be discovered. `SHA256SUMS.txt` does not list itself — measured: `grep -c SHA256SUMS SHA256SUMS.txt` is 0 — so it cannot certify its own content. If it stays, the hand-back says whether that is deliberate, what it means for a reader (the file can be stale about itself and nothing would say so), and whether anything covers it.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while verifying P13-T006, which is the second time this file has been found stale by hand. **A third instance was found on 2026-09-20 while accepting `P7-T012`:** commit `a217882` changed four files the manifest lists — `crates/sure-core/src/lib.rs`, `docs/architecture/CHECK_PIPELINE.md`, and `fixtures/adversarial/dynamic-not-authorized/scenario.json` and `fixtures/adversarial/intent-mismatch/scenario.json` — without updating it, and the worker who made the commit reported two of the four. The recurrence is the point of this task rather than an anecdote: three hand-found instances is enough to say the staleness is the normal state of the file and not a lapse, which is what "give it a reader, or take it out of the tree" is asking to decide. **And the regeneration is not in the tree either:** the supervisor updates the manifest with a scratch script under `target/tmp`, which is git-ignored, so the only maintainer of this file is a tool no reader of the repository can find. That is what makes this task's premise rather than its anecdote: the interval between "the manifest is stale" and "the manifest is stale again" is now measured in a single task, and a file that is wrong after almost every task that touches a listed path is not a file with a maintenance lapse. It is a file whose only maintainer is the supervisor's git-ignored scratch script, and the decision it asks for — give it a reader, or take it out of the tree — should be made on that basis. ADDED 2026-09-20 by the P15-T005 acceptance, a further measured instance of the same premise, this one with a mechanism. title: Put the test-count instrument where a contributor can run it, or stop producing counts by hand
acceptance: The premise is measured and the measurement is in the hand-back, not asserted from this task's notes. Three things are shown with the command that showed them: that `target/tmp/measure-run.mjs` is the only instrument in this repository that decides which of the two counts a figure is, that it is in no clone of the repository — `git ls-files --error-unmatch target/tmp/measure-run.mjs` fails, and `grep -rn measure-run` outside `target/` returns one file, `progress/HANDOFF.md`, which is prose about it rather than code that runs it — and that a wrong figure has been published after item 103 was written, not before it. A hand-back that repeats this task's sentence back is not a measurement.

The outcome is a decision and it is stated as one. Keeping the instrument outside the repository is the same defect `P15-T020` was minted for on `target/tmp/regen-sums.mjs`; the two are to be settled in the same direction rather than by accident in opposite ones, and if the decision here is to keep a script, the hand-back says what `P15-T020`'s answer will have to be for the repository to be consistent rather than leaving the second half to be discovered later.

If a script stays, it lives under `scripts/` and runs from a fresh clone with no setup beyond the files it measures, and it prints the two instruments and not one number. What each instrument is, is stated in the file: the parent figure is one `test <name> ... ok` line per test a parent ran, the raw sum is every `test result:` line, and the difference is produced by children that re-run a parent's test in a second process — which is why counting `test result:` lines over-counts and why the second instrument is a different question rather than a cross-check of the first.

It refuses rather than guesses, and the refusal path is exercised rather than reasoned about. When the two instruments disagree it prints no parent figure and exits non-zero, so a count that cannot be attributed cannot be quoted by whatever reads its output; the hand-back shows that path firing, on a log it constructs for the purpose, with the input and the output both in the record.

Wherever the number comes from, the next acceptance can produce its own from a fresh checkout and the file says how. `progress/state.json`'s evidence and `progress/HANDOFF.md`'s validation sections quote a passed count on every acceptance; the hand-back names the command that produces it after this task, and the sentence is specific enough that the next session runs it rather than describing it — a count produced by a procedure that exists only in `target/` is the situation this task exists to end, one level up.

Windows-primary and portable, as `CLAUDE.md` requires: it runs natively on Windows from PowerShell without Git Bash, and it does not require administrator rights, symlink privilege, or a Unix shell. If it is wired into CI or into the gate set, it runs on all three platforms and its cost is measured rather than assumed — and if it is not wired in, the hand-back gives the reason in writing, as the sixth gate's own header does for the choice it made.

The three figures this repository has already published wrong are re-derived rather than restated, so the hand-back is checked against the error it is about. `P15-T016` and `P13-T006` report raw sums where the parent counts are 2494 and 2508 on Windows; `P13-T007`'s hand-back commit message reports 2525 where the parent count is 2515, and six `cannot confirm` cells in a table it describes as having five. If the decision keeps a tool, the hand-back says what stops the next one, and `a rule in progress/HANDOFF.md` is not an answer: the rule was written down twice and the next occurrence was one commit later.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while accepting P13-T007. THE PREMISE, measured before the task was minted rather than inferred from item 103's prose: `target/tmp/measure-run.mjs` is the instrument item 103 records as built — it counts `test <name> ... ok` lines as one instrument and `raw sum − 10` as a second, and prints no parent figure at all when they disagree — and it is outside the repository. `git ls-files --error-unmatch target/tmp/measure-run.mjs` fails, and `grep -rn measure-run` finds one path outside `target/`: `progress/HANDOFF.md`, which describes it. No script under `scripts/`, no workflow under `.github/`, no test and no Rust file names it. THE ERROR IT DETECTS FIRED AGAIN ONE COMMIT AFTER ITEM 103 WAS WRITTEN. The `P13-T007` hand-back's commit message reports `2525 passed` beside `59 test binaries and 5 doc-test targets`; 2525 is the raw sum over that run's 74 `test result:` lines and the number of tests that exist is 2515, which is exactly the pair item 103 exists to keep apart. The same message says the new page's table has *five* `cannot confirm` cells and then enumerates one cursor cell, three Codex events and two Copilot event names, which is six; the page has six and a test that reads it enforces the three-value restriction mechanically. Item 103's falsifier was explicit — *the next validation that quotes a passed count without saying which of the two it is has to build the script instead of writing the rule down a third time* — and the script was built the same day, so what fired is narrower and more useful than the falsifier: the instrument exists and no one else can run it, which is the defect `P15-T020` names for `target/tmp/regen-sums.mjs` one artifact over. WHY A TASK AND NOT A ONE-LINE FIX IN THE ACCEPTANCE THAT FOUND IT: copying an unversioned script into `scripts/` is a deliverable change with a decision inside it — whether the count is produced by a committed tool, by `accept-task.mjs`, or by the gate run itself — and the identical choice is already open for the regeneration script under `P15-T020`, where the supervisor declined to settle it inside a verification note for the same reason. Settling one of the two by accident, inside an acceptance commit, would leave the repository holding two answers to one question, which is how the second half comes to be discovered later. PLACEMENT: after `P15-T020`, the last P15 task in array order, so §14 dispatches `P13-T009` next and the two unversioned instruments are settled in the order `tasks/tasks.json` lists them. NOT A STOP-THE-LINE: nothing here is a verdict about a user's project, and the cost of the gap is a wrong number in prose that this file corrects by hand each time it appears — which is the cost the task exists to stop paying, and the reason it is a task rather than a fourth sentence of rule.

title: Let a person make the grants that only their own file can make
acceptance: From a machine whose user has no settings file at all, a person reaches a run that reports the setting as in force, using only commands this build ships: a full recording written, or an execution mode other than `inspect_only` in the mode a run reports. Observed by running those commands and then reading what a later run says, not by reading the writer.

The location is named in the operating system's own terms, so a Windows user reads the path Explorer would show them, and it is named where it matters: in the confirmation the writing command prints, and in whatever a run says when a setting the person asked for is not in force.

What the command writes is read back by the same reader the product uses, proved by writing it and then having a hook or a check report the setting as the user's own rather than as a project's request — the same two answers `Authority::full_recording` and `Authority::execution_mode` give, observed from outside the process.

No path of this command reaches the project's own `sure.yaml`: with the working directory inside a project, the project's files are byte-for-byte what they were, and a request that names a project-level setting is refused rather than written into the project.

A setting that cannot take effect is not written silently: `telemetry`, which nothing implements, and a value this release refuses are either refused with the reason or written with the reason stated in the confirmation.
What the command prints when it changed something is a different sentence from what it prints when it changed nothing, so a person can tell a write from a no-op without opening the file.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while accepting P13-T009. THE HOLE THIS CLOSES WAS MADE BY CLOSING A BIGGER ONE. Until P13-T009 the only file that could turn a full recording on, or name an execution mode other than `inspect_only`, was the *project's* `sure.yaml` — which is the defect that task closed: a repository the user merely opened could turn the recording of their own machine's activity on, and could ask for its own code to be run. The grants now come from the user's own file alone (`Authority::full_recording`, `Authority::execution_mode`, and the resolution rule on the same method). That file has no writer and no reader a person can reach. It is named in this repository only as `Paths::user_config_file()` (`docs/architecture/CONFIG_REFERENCE.md`: 'outside any project, at `Paths::user_config_file()`'), `sure config show` is a stub, and MEASURED at P13-T009's acceptance on the supervisor's machine: `C:\Users\lishi\AppData\Roaming\SURE\sure.yaml` does not exist and nothing in this build creates it. THE CONSEQUENCE, STATED PLAINLY: full recording is now off for every user of this build, including a user who wants it, and the only way to turn it on is to hand-write YAML at a path the product names in Rust. The correct answer and the reachable answer have come apart, and that is priority 3 (plain-language UX) failing at the one place where the product's whole claim to authority lives. NOT OWNED ELSEWHERE: `P13-T008`'s 'Full recording off by default' is the criterion this change makes easier to meet rather than the writer; `P16-T006` is documentation; `P13-T010` is about allowances. Whether the fix is a `sure config` command, a file the product writes on request plus a `doctor` line, or a documented path in the user's own terms is the implementer's choice — what the acceptance asks for is that a person reaches the state without reading the source. PLACEMENT: after `P15-T021`, the last P15 task in array order, so this task cannot disturb the front of the READY list — which, measured when `P13-T009` was accepted, is `P13-T008` and not `P13-T010` as the pre-acceptance list suggested: `P13-T008` depends on `P13-T009`, so accepting that task is what made it READY.

title: Make the Copilot package, and the page that describes it, say what is true

notes: Minted 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while accepting P13-T009, from the two findings P13-T007's hand-back recorded and left unowned (that task's §5 and its HANDOFF section name them; this task is the owner they did not have). title: Decide which text the goal report shows, and make the sentence true either way
acceptance: `sure check --goal "..."` and the record the same command wrote agree: either the report prints the text the store holds, or the goal is exempted from the store's redaction and the document that says 'minus nothing' is the one that is right — and which of the two won is stated in the commit message and in the document, not left to a reader to infer.

The sentence `Your goal was written to the history as record N` is never printed over a record whose text is not the text shown beside it. Observed by running the command with a credential in the goal and comparing the report byte for byte against every byte under the store directory, not by reading the code.

Whichever way it is decided, `crates/sure-core/src/store/mod.rs`'s rule that every accepted document is redacted has one stated exception at most, and the exception names the goal alone rather than opening a general door.

The corpus entry `a-secret-typed-into-a-goal-reaches-the-store-only-redacted` in `fixtures/privacy/manifest.json` becomes an assertion about the report as well as the store, and the corresponding entry in that file's `not_confirmed` is removed rather than left to describe a gap that no longer exists.

No credential typed into `--goal` reaches a surface the user did not type it into: a report captured, redirected to a file or read by a harness holds the redacted form, or the decision above says why that is not the rule.
notes: Minted 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while accepting P13-T008, from the first of the three entries P13-T008's corpus recorded in `fixtures/privacy/manifest.json`'s `not_confirmed` with `owner: unassigned`. That task was right to record it and right not to decide it: the two rules in collision are both deliberate, and which one wins is a product decision rather than a test's. MEASURED BY P13-T008, not by the supervisor: the case `a-secret-typed-into-a-goal-reaches-the-store-only-redacted` asserts the store half and passes — every byte under the store directory holds `deploy using token *** please` and no byte holds the credential — while the command prints the goal verbatim under the sentence 'Your goal was written to the history as record N'. The two surfaces are `crates/sure-cli/src/check.rs` (the sentence and the verbatim text) and `crates/sure-core/src/store/mod.rs` (`redact_document`, applied to every document a write accepts). The collision is with `docs/product/PROJECT_INTENT.md`, which says the text is stored verbatim -- 'minus nothing'. WHY THIS IS NOT A COSMETIC INCONSISTENCY: the report has a machine form, so a credential typed into `--goal` travels in a JSON report a harness may capture or log, and the sentence beside it explicitly claims the report and the history agree. A reader who believes the sentence concludes the secret is only in a redacted record. NOT MEASURED HERE: whether any other report surface echoes unredacted text on the same pattern — this task is the goal, and a sweep for the same shape elsewhere would be its own finding rather than this task's silent expansion.

title: Let a caller name the settings file, so the consent path can be tested at all
acceptance: A caller can point one SURE run at a named user settings file by a documented flag or environment variable, the way `--store-dir` already names the store, and a run that names one loads that file and no other.

The flag is not a way to escalate: a named settings file cannot grant more than the user's real file could, a project's own files cannot set or redirect it, and the agent-facing paths — hooks, the MCP server, anything a project can influence — either ignore it or refuse it, proved by a test that tries.

`fixtures/privacy/manifest.json`'s `not_confirmed` entry `no-recording-through-the-binary` is removed, and the case it names becomes a driven entry at `layer: binary`: a real `sure` process, pointed at a settings file that grants full recording, writes a recording and the corpus asserts it by reading every byte under the store directory.

The suite's premise test — that this machine has no settings file of its own — keeps passing and keeps being about the real path rather than the named one, so the default case and the consented case are both observed and both distinguished from 'the test moved the location and forgot'.

`docs/` says where the named settings file is read, what it may grant, and that it is a testing and automation surface rather than a user-facing one, and `sure doctor` reports which settings file a run used.
notes: Minted 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while accepting P13-T008, from the second of the three entries P13-T008's corpus recorded in `fixtures/privacy/manifest.json`'s `not_confirmed`, there with `owner: unassigned`. THE GAP IS REAL AND IT IS NOT P13-T008'S TO CLOSE: full-recording consent comes from the user's own settings file alone (`Authority::full_recording`), on Windows that is `%APPDATA%\SURE\sure.yaml` resolved through `SHGetKnownFolderPath`, `Paths::discover_at` moves the store and not the settings, and no test may write the settings of the person running the suite — so P13-T008 drove its consent case at the store layer and said so, which is the honest response to an untestable seam. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, and the reason this is worth a task rather than a shrug: acceptance line 1 of P13-T008 ('Full recording off by default') is observable only in its negative half. The positive half — a real process opening a recording because a user granted one — has never been executed end to end in this repository, and cannot be until a caller can name the file. RELATION TO P15-T022, which is a different hole in the same wall: that task is that nothing *writes* the user's file, so the grant has no producer; this one is that nothing can *read a different one*, so the grant has no test. A flag closes this and would make that one easier to verify, but neither is a fix for the other and this task does not claim P15-T022. THE ESCALATION CLAUSE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: a caller-named settings path is exactly the shape of a privilege-laundering surface in a product whose rule is that a project cannot decide what SURE may do to the machine, so acceptance line 2 is written as a refusal to prove rather than a promise to keep. NOT MEASURED HERE: which of a flag and an environment variable is the right one, and whether the hooks must refuse it outright or may accept it — that is this task's decision and should be argued in its commit message.

title: Make the product-eval numbers measured, or stop stating them

title: Decide what a browser-launch timeout means, before raising the budget a third time
acceptance: The question is answered with evidence rather than by raising the number again: `crates/sure-core/tests/browser_driver.rs`'s launch budget has been raised twice already (10 -> 20 seconds, then 20 -> 30), each time because a launch consumed the whole budget on a loaded CI runner, and the third occurrence has now happened at the third ceiling. The hand-back states what the reported duration can and cannot distinguish, measured from the code rather than reasoned about, and says whether the budget is raised again, replaced by a rule, or left alone — with the argument for the choice.

The tautology is dealt with. `LaunchError::NeverOpened`'s `waited` is not a measurement of the browser, it is what was left of the caller's budget when the launch began (`session.rs:838-842` computes `left` by subtracting the elapsed search from `limits.timeout()`, and `launch.rs:258-266` reports that same figure after polling to `Instant::now() >= deadline`), so the message can only ever say that the deadline was reached. Either the figure is replaced by something that distinguishes a launch that was still making progress from one that was not — the child's liveness, its stderr, the profile directory's state — or the message says plainly that the browser was still running at the deadline and that how close it was is not known.

Whether the process was alive at the deadline is observed rather than assumed. The loop already calls `child.try_wait()` and returns `Exited` when the browser has stopped, so a `NeverOpened` is a browser that was still running; the hand-back says what that does and does not rule out, and what the recorded complaints (`dbus/bus.cc` errors on ubuntu) mean for the three machines the suite runs on.

The never-vacuous contract survives. `opened()` in that file refuses to pass over the case where a browser was found and could not be driven, on the stated ground that this is the one machine state in which the acceptance sentence *the check can navigate a local app* is never exercised. Whatever changes, a run in which a browser is present and is never driven still fails, and still prints which contract the machine's state was checked against — the failure may not be converted into an absence, a skip, or a `continue-on-error`.

The three occurrences are named with their run ids and their figures, read from the CI logs rather than from the comments that record the earlier two: `35196110213` (windows, `19.999018`), `35365324422` (ubuntu, `19.999964`), `35351409364` (windows, `29.999205` and `29.999266`), and `35407533960` (ubuntu, `29.999916`, on commit `4b190e6`, where the next run of the identical tree was green on the same platform). Any further occurrence found in the branch's run history is named too, and if none is found that is stated as the bound of the search rather than left open.
notes: Added 2026-09-19 by the supervisor while accepting P13-T008, from a red CI run on the acceptance commit itself. The failing test is `crates/sure-core/tests/browser_driver.rs:397`'s `a_page_that_never_arrives_is_a_failure_of_the_project_and_not_an_absence`, panicking with `a browser was found at /usr/bin/chromium and could not be driven: Absence { reason: DriverWouldNotStart, detail: "/usr/bin/chromium ran for 29.999916 seconds without reporting a debugging port, and said: ... Failed to connect to the bus ..." }`. It is NOT P13-T008's: that task's `crates/sure-cli/tests/privacy_suite.rs` ran on the same ubuntu job and passed 6 tests, 0 failed, in 0.10s, and the other four jobs including all of windows and macos are green. The same tree one commit later (`95f3da5`, a progress-only commit) is green on ubuntu, 40 minutes after, which is what makes this a flake rather than a defect of the tree — and it is the second time this acceptance has had to distinguish those two. WHY IT IS STILL WORTH A TASK: `P15-T016`'s notes name this exact cause first among three and say it 'must be characterised rather than assumed fixed'; `P15-T016` was accepted without that characterisation, and the file's own comments show the pattern it should have been characterised into — the budget has been raised twice on this evidence (the `PATIENT` comment cites `35351409364` at `29.999205`/`29.999266`, the `BRIEF` comment cites `35365324422` at `19.999964` and `35196110213` at `19.999018`), and the third occurrence has now landed at the third ceiling. THE MEASUREMENT THAT MAKES THE THIRD RAISE UNJUSTIFIED BY DEFAULT, taken from the source rather than from the message: the duration printed is not how long the browser took, it is how much of the caller's budget was left when the launch started (`session.rs:838-842`) reported after polling to the deadline (`launch.rs:221`, `:258-266`, `:263`), so it is bounded above by the budget by construction and would read the same for a browser one millisecond from writing its port and for one that was never going to. Raising the budget a third time is therefore a guess dressed as a measurement, and the honest options are to make the failure observable (what was the child doing at the deadline?) or to stop implying the figure measures the browser.
