title: Stop the acceptance report creating scratch inside the shipped fixture tree
acceptance: After the acceptance report runs, `fixtures/adversarial/dynamic-not-authorized` holds nothing that was not already there: observed by running the report and then WALKING THE FILESYSTEM, not by reading `execution_refusal`. The reason the walk is required rather than merely preferred is the shape of the residue — it is EMPTY DIRECTORIES, and git does not describe directories at all, so `git status` cannot show them at any verbosity. A check written as `git status`, or as an existence test on a path, would pass both before and after the fix and would prove nothing. `git status --untracked-files=all` still belongs in the check, because it is what would catch a run that goes on to write a FILE; the walk is what catches the directories. Both are run and both are reported, and the check says which one is watching for which. The two directories that exist today are gone from a tree that has run it, and a fresh checkout that runs it does not acquire them.

A mutation that puts the scratch back under `fixtures_root` makes that check redden, run, with its literal output reported. If it does not redden, the check is describing the code rather than testing it.

The configuration roots are still created, still empty, and still are not the machine's own configuration directory, so the case still measures what it measured: the fixture's own `sure.yaml` is the file that asks for more, and `Paths::from_roots` is still given two directories that exist. If moving the scratch changes the measurement, say so and explain it rather than adjusting the expectation to match.

The replacement location is stated in the code with its reason, and the reason is not convenience: this repository keeps scratch under `target/tmp`, which is git-ignored and on the same volume as the checkout, and the nearest in-repo precedent for clearing a path before using it is `crates/sure-core/tests/doctor.rs:46-67` — read its header before copying it, because it records that its own concurrency mechanism "was not confirmed".

Nothing else about the case changes. `dynamic-not-authorized` still produces the same measurement it produced before, and if the report's own text about this case changes, the change is named rather than left for a reader to find.
notes:
MINTED FROM A SUPERVISOR-READ FILE, NOT FROM A REPORT ABOUT IT. `crates/sure-core/src/acceptance_report.rs` is shipped code — 2,532 lines with zero `#[cfg(test)]`, zero `#[test]` and zero `mod tests` at `96c490b`, declared `pub mod acceptance_report;` from `lib.rs` — and its `execution_refusal` creates directories inside the SHIPPED FIXTURE TREE. The anchors below were read at `96c490b`; `acceptance_report.rs` is being edited by another task as this is written, so re-read rather than trusting the numbers.



WHAT IT DOES. `fn execution_refusal(fixtures_root: &Path, id: &str)` takes `let root = fixtures_root.join(id)` (`:1504`) and then builds `let scratch = root.join("target").join("tmp").join("acceptance report configuration")` (`:1510-1513`), creating `scratch/data` and `scratch/config` with `create_dir_all` at `:1516-1519`. `fixtures_root` is not a scratch area: it is `repository_root.join(FIXTURES_PATH)` (`:608`), and `execution_refusal` is called as `execution_refusal(fixtures_root, id)` (`:969`). The module's own comment at `:1505-1509` says why the directories are created — `Paths::from_roots` "validates both roots and creates neither" — and that reasoning is sound; what is wrong is where they are put.



WHY IT IS A DEFECT AND NOT A PREFERENCE. (1) The fixture is shipped bytes: `fixtures/adversarial/dynamic-not-authorized` is tracked, six files, and the repository states the discipline in words at `crates/sure-core/tests/repair_fixture_e2e.rs:73-77` — *"It does not run the shipped directory, and it does not write to it: every run happens on a copy under `target/tmp`"*. This module writes to it instead. (2) It is not ignored: `git check-ignore -v` on the created path exits 1, and nothing under `fixtures/` carries a `.gitignore`; the root `/target/` entry is anchored and does not reach `fixtures/adversarial/<id>/target/`. The residue is invisible today only because git does not track empty directories — `fixtures/adversarial/dynamic-not-authorized/target/tmp/acceptance report configuration/{config,data}` exists on disk right now, and both are empty. (3) The moment anything writes a file there — and the directories are handed to `Paths::from_roots` as a configuration root — it becomes an untracked file inside a shipped fixture. (4) The measurement stops being idempotent, which matters more than the residue: the pipeline is then run over `&root`, so the fixture is measured with two directories in it that an earlier run created. A case whose subject changes each time it is observed is not measuring the same thing twice.



HOW FAR IT REACHES, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT VAGUE. `execution_refusal` is reached only through `Some(Recipe::ExecutionRefusal)` (`:969`), the case `("dynamic-not-authorized", Recipe::ExecutionRefusal)` (`:491`). The only callers of `acceptance_report` in the tree are `crates/sure-core/tests/acceptance_report_runner.rs` and `crates/sure-core/tests/release_gate_runner.rs`; no `sure-cli` caller exists, so this is public API exercised only by tests and is not yet on the binary's path. That bounds the blast radius. It does not make it harmless — it is one `pub` call away, and it already leaves residue on any machine that has run the suite.



TWO PRECEDENTS EXIST FOR THE FIX, AND NEITHER CAN BE CALLED FROM THIS MODULE AS IT STANDS. The repository already has the right discipline in two places. `crates/sure-cli/src/hook.rs:937-943`'s `scratch_hook_dir(name)` builds `repository_root()/target/tmp/<name>/<pid>`. `crates/sure-core/src/store/mod.rs:1088-1094`'s `scratch_root()` derives the same root from `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")` and two parents "rather than the working directory, so a test gives the same answer wherever it was started from", and its reasoning is written out at `:1103-1116`: the name carries the process id because *"freshness must not depend on a deletion succeeding, because on Windows a file another process holds cannot be deleted and the failure is easy to swallow"*. Both build the path with `PathBuf::join` and never touch a string, which is why neither is exposed to the whitespace and non-ASCII names that already exist under `target/tmp` — read both before choosing a location.



The wrinkle that will catch whoever implements this: `scratch_root` is `#[cfg(test)] pub(crate)`, and `acceptance_report.rs` is **shipped** code with no `#[cfg(test)]` anywhere in its 2,532 lines. It therefore cannot call `scratch_root` without either failing to build into the shipped library or making test infrastructure part of the public API — and the second is worse than the duplication it avoids. Derive the path the way `scratch_root` does, and write in the code why the duplication is deliberate rather than an oversight. This is also the reason the task is not simply "move the call": there is no existing non-test helper to move it to.



WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. No file has been written into the fixture by this path: `store: None` is passed to the pipeline at `:1531`, so no store is opened, and the two directories are created empty and stay empty. The exposure today is five empty directories, not corrupted bytes. Do not restate this task as "the fixtures are being modified" — say what was measured.

title: Make a saturated re-check scan fail closed, or say it did not read far enough
acceptance: A scan that stops at its bound is never reported as "nothing was left open": observed by driving the read into saturation and reporting what a reader is told. Neither an empty list nor a reassurance is an acceptable answer to a scan that stopped early, and the check that establishes this drives the bound rather than arguing about it.

The direction chosen matches `Store::spend_allowance`, or the difference is stated with its reason. `spend_allowance` reads its bound at `store/mod.rs:583` and returns `None` when the scan saturates, and `None` means spend nothing, so it fails closed. Whichever way this read goes — refuse, or succeed while reporting the truncation — the choice is written where a reader finds it, and the plain-language plumbing that already exists (`pipeline.rs` turns an `Err` here into `StageOutcome::NotRun` with a detail) is used rather than a second mechanism invented beside it.

The doc comment at `recheck_lifecycle.rs:225-236` describes what the code does. It presently claims the number is chosen "in the shape of `allowance::SCAN_LIMIT` and for the same reason" and that a store reaching it "has something wrong with it, which is exactly what `allowance::SCAN_LIMIT` says about its own" — the final clause is false about behaviour, because allowance detects saturation and acts on it while this read does not. The supervisor HAS corrected it, in the `P7-T012` acceptance commit, before this task was dispatched — so say so and do not re-correct it. What that correction could not do is check the bound, because the read has no check to add one to; that is this task.

The saturation is reachable by a test. Either a store is filled past the bound, or the scan takes its bound as a parameter so a test can set it to a small number, or the bound read is otherwise driven directly — and the shape chosen is stated with its reason. A test that cannot reach the branch it is about is not evidence about that branch.

What the bound does not affect is stated rather than left to be rediscovered: nothing consumes `LifecycleUpdate::findings` today, so saturation understates the `Against the earlier run: N finding(s) still open` line and stage 12's detail rather than the verdict's own findings. If that has changed, say what now consumes it and what the consequence is.
notes:
MINTED BY THE SUPERVISOR WHILE ACCEPTING `P7-T012`, FROM A QUESTION THAT TASK DID NOT ASK. `P7-T012` fixed a real defect — `recheck_lifecycle.rs` passed `0` to `Store::history`, which documents `0` as "return none", so the read that finds what an earlier run left open could only ever answer "nothing". It replaced `0` with `HISTORY_SCAN_LIMIT: usize = 4096`. That is a strict improvement and this task does not dispute it. What it left unexamined is what happens when the new bound is *reached*.

THE DEFECT. `previous_open_findings` (`recheck_lifecycle.rs:289-319`) builds a filter carrying only a kind, calls `store.history(&filter, HISTORY_SCAN_LIMIT)` at `:300`, filters to this project in Rust at `:304`, and returns `Ok(findings)` at `:318`. There is no check of whether the scan saturated. Read at `a217882`; the supervisor read this file rather than taking it from a report. **The anchors in this note are the `a217882` tree's.** The `P7-T012` acceptance commit corrected the doc sentence criterion 3 is about, which added twelve lines above `HISTORY_SCAN_LIMIT`, so on the tree this task will actually be dispatched against every anchor at or below the old line 237 is twelve higher: `previous_open_findings` is `:289-319` rather than `:277-307`, the bound is passed at `:300` rather than `:288`, the project filter runs at `:304`, `Ok(findings)` returns at `:318`, and the doc block criterion 3 names is `:225-248`. `LifecycleUpdate` at `:71` is above the shift and is unchanged.

WHY THAT IS A FALSE GREEN AND NOT A BOUND. A saturated scan returns a list that is short for a reason the caller cannot see, and an empty one is indistinguishable from the true and reassuring answer "no earlier run left anything open". The distinction this repository ranks above every other — *"A false green is more serious than a visible error"* — is exactly the one this return value erases.

THE PRECEDENT IT CITES DOES THE OPPOSITE, AND THAT IS THE SHARPEST WAY TO SEE IT. The doc at `recheck_lifecycle.rs:225-248` says the number is chosen "in the shape of `crate::allowance::SCAN_LIMIT` and for the same reason", ending "a store that reaches it has something wrong with it, which is exactly what `allowance::SCAN_LIMIT` says about its own". The last clause is false about behaviour. `Store::spend_allowance` reads its bound and then ACTS on it — `store/mod.rs:582-585`, verified at `a217882`:

```rust
let rows = self.history(&filter, allowance::SCAN_LIMIT)?;
if rows.len() >= allowance::SCAN_LIMIT {
    return Ok(None);
}
```

`None` means spend nothing, so an exhausted allowance fails **closed**: it refuses rather than guessing. `previous_open_findings` has no equivalent, so it fails **open**. For an allowance, reaching the bound makes SURE *do less*, which is safe. For this read, reaching the bound makes SURE *claim less is wrong*, which is not. The number is the same and the failure direction is opposite, so "for the same reason" is true of the justification and false of the consequence. The `P7-T012` worker confirmed on being asked that it did not consider detecting the bound, and that the sentence overclaims; it is that worker's sentence and its correction is credited to it.

THE FIX ALREADY HAS ITS PLUMBING, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A SMALL TASK AND NOT A DESIGN. `pipeline.rs:1098-1112` already turns an `Err` from this read into `StageOutcome::NotRun { reason: UnknownReason, detail: "SURE could not read what an earlier run left open: {error}" }`. So failing closed is a matter of returning an error instead of a short list, and the report already knows how to say so in plain language. The alternative — succeed but report that the scan stopped early — is also open, and is a choice about what a re-check should do when its history cannot be read. **That choice is the task.** The stronger fix, which does not remove the need for detection, is to stop spending the budget on other projects' rows: `HistoryFilter` carries `project_fingerprint` but no `project_root`, so pushing the project filter into the query would let the limit count this project's rows rather than the store's. Whether that API change belongs here or in its own task is the implementer's call, stated in the code.

THE BLAST RADIUS, BOUNDED RATHER THAN DRAMATISED. Nothing consumes `LifecycleUpdate::findings` today: the type is declared at `recheck_lifecycle.rs:71`, produced by `pipeline::recheck` (`:1084`), and carried on `RunOutcome.lifecycle` (`pipeline.rs:461`), while the readers the worker traced — `check.rs:575-590`, `:877-890`, `pipeline.rs:1147-1148` — read only `kept_open` and `resolved`, or their lengths. So saturation today understates the `Against the earlier run: N finding(s) still open` line and stage 12's detail; it does not move `run.verdict.findings`, the open-finding counts, or hand-off readiness. Criterion 5 exists because that bound on the damage is exactly what would change if that field gained a consumer, and whoever gives it one inherits this.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED, AND IT MATTERS FOR HOW URGENT THIS IS. That saturation is reachable in practice. No fixture or test saturates the store; 4096 is a judgement about scale, and neither the `P7-T012` worker nor the supervisor found a case that reaches it. The worker said so rather than letting the number imply a measurement, and this task repeats it. What is false today, independently of reachability, is the doc sentence in criterion 3. The behavioural question is real but unmeasured, and criterion 4 is what turns it into a measurement instead of leaving it as a worry.

title: Decide what makes two project paths the same project, before the tier is counted from them
acceptance: The claim is measured before anything is changed, and the measurement is the one this task was minted from rather than a restatement of it: one store, one recorded session, one `sure check` command, and the project named four ways — as the hook recorded it, with forward slashes, with an upper-case drive and user, with a trailing separator, and with a `.` segment. All five lines are quoted with the command that produced them. Today the first reports `(capability tier 1, observed)` and counted 4 events, and the other four report `(capability tier 0, snapshot)` and `SURE counted no session events for this project: SURE's store holds none for it. SURE also read 4 session events recorded for other projects`. Every one of the last four names one directory that Windows treats as the same directory as the first.

The mechanism is chosen rather than assumed, and it says at the decision what it asks, what it does when it cannot tell, and which way it errs when it cannot tell. `crates/sure-core/src/capability_report.rs` compares `record.project_root.as_deref() == Some(project_root)` — string equality — so the answer is a spelling of a path rather than the identity of a directory. `crates/sure-core/src/recheck_lifecycle.rs:57-67`'s `normalise_path` is the repository's existing attempt at this question and folds case under `#[cfg(windows)]`; read it, and read `P15-T018`, which owns that function and says why the operating system is not the authority — case sensitivity belongs to the volume. A normalisation chosen here must not contradict the answer `P15-T018` lands on for findings, or SURE will hold two different opinions about when two paths are one project.

The direction of the error is stated as a verdict-level effect and is measured, not reasoned. Getting this wrong in one direction understates — SURE counts nothing for a directory it has a session for, which is today's defect and is the safe direction. Getting it wrong in the other direction OVERSTATES: a normalisation too eager makes two genuinely different projects compare equal, and this project's report would then count another project's events as its own. That is a false green in the product's own voice and is the failure this task must not introduce. The hand-back says what the chosen mechanism does when the two paths cannot be resolved, and which way that errs.

A test pins the behaviour on every platform and is not structurally blind. The existing test cannot catch this defect: `crates/sure-cli/src/check.rs`'s `the_tier_in_a_check_report_is_the_one_the_projects_events_earn` records the session with the same `root` string it later checks, so both sides of the comparison are the identical spelling and any normalisation passes it. The new test names the project at least two ways that reach one directory, asserts they report the same tier, and says what it is asking the platform where that is not universal — the pattern `P15-T016` landed in `candidate_context` and `recheck_lifecycle`. A loosened or removed assertion is not an answer.

Anything that cannot be run on the machine this loop develops on is reported as not measured rather than inferred, and the safe direction is preserved where the mechanism cannot decide. A case-insensitive fold is right on Windows and on a default macOS volume and wrong on a case-sensitive one; if the mechanism cannot tell which it is looking at, it must err toward counting fewer events and saying so, never toward counting another project's.
notes:
MINTED FROM THE SUPERVISOR'S OWN MEASUREMENT WHILE ACCEPTING `P7-T013`, not from a report about it. Every line below was observed at `3beebbd` with `target/debug/sure.exe` hashed before and after the runs (sha256 `2312b78f80699aa8c29dbc3d96a48b14…`, identical at both ends), against a scratch store under `target/tmp` holding one four-event Codex session for the project. The user's real store was not touched.

WHAT IT DOES. `crates/sure-core/src/capability_report.rs`'s `for_project` partitions the store's event records into "this project's" and "other projects'" with `record.project_root.as_deref() == Some(project_root)` — a string comparison — and the tier, the counted sentence and the blind spots all follow from which side of that partition the records land on. So the report's answer is a fact about how the path was SPELLED, not about which directory it names.

MEASURED, one command each, same store, same directory:

| how the project was named | what the report said |
|---|---|
| as the hook recorded it | `(capability tier 1, observed) SURE counted 4 session events recorded for this project by codex, between 2026-09-20T09:13:16.240Z and 2026-09-20T09:13:16.676Z.` |
| with forward slashes | `(capability tier 0, snapshot) SURE counted no session events for this project: SURE's store holds none for it. SURE also read 4 session events recorded for other projects; they are not part of this project's tier and were not counted.` |
| upper-case drive and user | the same tier-0 line |
| trailing separator | the same tier-0 line |
| a `.` segment inside the path | the same tier-0 line |

The machine form agrees, which is why this is not a wording problem: on the mismatched spelling `--format json` reports `{"tier":0,"blind_spots":["no_session_visibility","no_pre_action_control"],"evidence":{"elsewhere":4,"events":0,…}}` — four records read, none counted, and the four attributed to other projects.

WHY IT IS A DEFECT AND NOT A PREFERENCE. On Windows those five spellings name one directory. A user who copies a path out of a tool that writes forward slashes, or who types a drive letter in the case their keyboard produced, is checking the project SURE has a session for and is told SURE has never seen it. The failure is silent in the sense that matters: the sentence is confident and specific — "SURE's store holds none for it" — and it is false. It is a false statement about the store rather than a missing one, which is worse than saying nothing.

THE DIRECTION IS SAFE TODAY, AND THAT IS NOT A REASON TO LEAVE IT. Every mismatching spelling UNDERSTATES: the tier falls to 0 and the notice names the events it did not count, so a careful reader can diagnose it. Nothing here claims more than SURE can prove. That is exactly why this is a task with its own acceptance rather than a stop-the-line, and it is also why the fix needs care rather than enthusiasm: the same comparison, normalised too eagerly, starts counting ANOTHER project's events as this one's, and the tier would rise on evidence that is not about this project at all. Understating is a defect; overstating is a false green, and the fix must not trade one for the other.

THE PRECEDENT IS IN THE TREE AND IS NOT FREE TO COPY. `recheck_lifecycle::normalise_path` (`crates/sure-core/src/recheck_lifecycle.rs:57-67`) folds case under `#[cfg(windows)]` and changes nothing elsewhere, and it is what decides whether a previous finding matches this run's finding. It also does not answer the separator, trailing-separator or dot-segment cases at all, so copying it would fix one of the four measured spellings. `P15-T018` — *"Ask the volume, not the operating system, whether two paths are one file"* — owns that function and is where the repository has already decided that the operating system is not the authority on case, because case sensitivity belongs to the volume. This task and that one must land on the same answer or SURE will hold two opinions about when two paths are one thing; read `P15-T018`'s note before choosing a mechanism, and record in this task whichever way it goes.

THE INTENDED BEHAVIOUR IS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN AND IS NOT HONOURED. `--store-dir` refuses a relative path with a sentence that states this task's whole principle — *"A relative path would be resolved against the current directory, so whether it is inside the project would depend on where SURE happened to be started."* The product already refuses to let a path's meaning depend on where it was written. The comparison this task is about lets a path's meaning depend on how it was typed, which is the same defect one level down.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. No file is corrupted, no store is damaged, and nothing here is a security boundary. The exposure is a wrong and confident sentence about a project's recorded history, plus a tier that is lower than the truth. Both are the product being unsure in a place where it has the evidence to be sure — which is the thing this repository exists to stop.

title: Test the installer against the archive the build produces, not a fixture that agrees with it
acceptance: The gap is confirmed before anything is changed, and it is confirmed by reading the two sides rather than by restating this note: `scripts/Build-Release.ps1` is the only thing in the tree that produces `sure-<version>-<target>.zip`, and `crates/sure-cli/tests/install_flow.rs` never runs it — its `STAGE_AND_PACK` script builds its own archive in the same layout. Say in the hand-back what the fixture and the build produce, field by field, and name every difference, including the ones that are legitimately absent from the fixture (a real `sure.exe` built in release mode, the version string, the `logs\` and `scratch\` directories the build writes beside the archive).

A test drives the installer against an archive the build actually produced, or the reason it cannot is measured and recorded. The supervisor's acceptance run for `P15-T003` is the existence proof that this is possible on this machine: `scripts/Build-Release.ps1` packaged `sure-0.0.0-bootstrap-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` (4045010 bytes, sha256 `2fb0d05f8c903a159198e031dd9cb35d111172492c013632784a7d8b7761015f`) into `target/tmp/release/`, and `scripts/Install-Sure.ps1` installed it at exit 0. If the test cannot run the build itself — because it needs `target/tmp/release-gate.json` and takes minutes — then it must consume an archive the build produced, and it must say what it does when none is there. A test that silently skips is not a test: this repository has already recorded that a skipped check is not a pass.

The failure this task exists to catch is shown reddening. Take the one thing the fixture cannot get wrong because it is written beside the installer — the `.sha256` line's format, the archive's single top-level directory, the payload names — and change one of them in the build's output or in the installer's expectation, and show the new test failing while the old fixture-based suite still passes. That pair of readings is the whole point of the task: it is the measurement that a drift between the two sides is invisible today.

Whatever the test ends up costing is stated rather than hidden, and the six gates still pass. If the answer is a test that runs the build, say how long it adds and whether it belongs in the default `cargo test` run or behind a label. `CLAUDE.md` requires the Rust core to stay portable to macOS and Linux, so a Windows-only test must be gated the way the rest of the Windows-only flow is, and must not make the non-Windows jobs fail.
notes:
MINTED FROM THE SUPERVISOR'S OWN ACCEPTANCE OF `P15-T003`, out of a limit that task recorded rather than from a report about it.

WHAT THE GAP IS. `P15-T003` ships `scripts/Install-Sure.ps1`, whose input contract is the archive `scripts/Build-Release.ps1` produces: one top-level directory of the archive's own name, holding `sure.exe`, `LICENSE` and `RELEASE.txt`, with a `<archive>.sha256` beside it in `sha256sum` format. `crates/sure-cli/tests/install_flow.rs` tests that contract thoroughly — 13 tests, both PowerShell hosts, a real MCP handshake through the installed binary — against an archive **it builds itself**, from a `STAGE_AND_PACK` script that writes the layout the installer expects. Both sides of the contract are therefore asserted by one author in one file. If `Build-Release.ps1` changed the payload names, nested the directory, renamed the checksum file or wrote a CRLF line, `install_flow` would stay green and a user's install would fail.

WHY THIS IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL, AND WHY IT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS LAST TIME. `P15-T002` was accepted with exactly this defect in it: `-Phase Verify` failed for the only person who would ever run it — someone holding a downloaded archive — and every gate was green, because no test ran the phase the way that person does. The supervisor found it while accepting, not while testing. The install flow is the same surface one step further along, and the fixture is the same kind of substitute: faithful to the author's understanding, and unable to disagree with it.

WHAT WAS MEASURED, AT ACCEPTANCE. Two facts, both in `P15-T003`'s evidence:

| | |
|---|---|
| the build's archive, installed for real | `Build-Release.ps1`'s `sure-0.0.0-bootstrap-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip`, 4045010 bytes, sha256 `2fb0d05f8c903a159198e031dd9cb35d111172492c013632784a7d8b7761015f`, installed by `Install-Sure.ps1 -InstallRoot` into a scratch root: **exit 0**, `bin\sure.exe` 9089536 bytes sha256 `483d2769…`, the user's planted `sure.db` unchanged |
| what the test suite installs | an archive `install_flow.rs` stages itself, from `STAGE_AND_PACK` — payload bytes are the cargo-built `target/debug/sure.exe`, `LICENSE` and `RELEASE.txt` are literal fixture strings, and the `.sha256` is written by the same script |

So the behaviour is verified once, by hand, against the real thing — and the suite that is supposed to keep it verified is verified against a stand-in.

WHAT THE TASK IS NOT. It is not "make the fixture more realistic" — a fixture cannot disagree with the code it was written beside, however detailed it gets. It is not a request to run a multi-minute build inside `cargo test` either; the acceptance allows the honest answer to be "consume an archive the build produced, and fail loudly when there is none", which is what `P15-T002`'s `-Phase Verify` does with the release gate. What it must not be is a check that quietly does nothing when the archive is absent, because a skipped dynamic check is not a pass and this repository has said so since before this task existed.

RELATED. `P15-T011` creates the release workflow and its checksums, and will produce this archive in CI; whatever this task lands should be readable from there. `P15-T004` builds the WinGet manifest over the same artifact and inherits the same naming contract.

title: Give the store a location a caller can choose
acceptance: A caller can name where SURE keeps its store, and `sure doctor` reports the location it is using. The mechanism is not project-controlled: a store that a checked project's own file could redirect is a store that a checked project could point at a place it can write.

No test in the workspace writes to the per-user store. `crates/sure-cli/tests/cli_contract.rs::hook_ingest_reads_standard_input_and_evaluates_protection` runs a real `sure hook ingest`, and that process opens and writes the developer's `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SURE\sure.db` (measured: 4096 bytes added by one isolated run, rows of kind `event` with session `cursor-session-001`). After this task the store is byte-identical across a full `cargo test --workspace`, asserted by a test rather than by a report.
The default is unchanged: a caller who names nothing gets the OS-native per-user location through the existing path abstraction, and `sure doctor` still reports it.
A location inside the project being checked is refused, as it already is on the `--goal` path, and the refusal says what did not happen.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P7-T010's verification. Running `cargo test --workspace` on this repository writes rows into the developer's own store, and the per-user directory is read through `SHGetKnownFolderPath`, which ignores `LOCALAPPDATA`, so there is no environment variable a test can set to point a spawned SURE elsewhere. `docs/architecture/CLI.md` already described this as "the phase that gives SURE a store location a caller can choose"; no such task existed, so the gap had no owner and every gate run added to the history of the machine it ran on.

title: Carry a finding through the repair contract and the re-check
acceptance: `sure repair` on a project with an open finding answers with a repair contract, and a later `sure recheck` reports what that run left open — both observed by running the commands, not by a report about them.

The re-check list comes from the module that owns the rule (`sure_core::repair_impact`), not from a second rule written in the pipeline. `RepairContract::from_finding` refuses an empty re-check list, and that refusal is met by selecting the checks first rather than bypassed with a hand-built contract that is not actionable.

Findings are persisted, so `recheck_lifecycle::store_run` gains its caller and a second run's stage 12 compares against a real earlier run instead of an always-empty history. `recheck_lifecycle.rs`'s `store.history(&filter, 0)` call is fixed with it: `Store::history` documents 0 as "return none", so the read that is meant to find previous open findings can only ever return empty.
Stages 11 and 12 stop being `not_run` on a project that has findings, and any stage that still did not run is named in the report.
`docs/architecture/CLI.md` and `docs/architecture/CHECK_PIPELINE.md` match what the two commands do, including the status each returns.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P7-T010's verification. P7-T010 records stage 11 as not-run and passes `rechecks: &[]` to stage 12, each with a written reason: `RepairContract::from_finding` needs the checks that can observe a finding, `repair_impact::select_impacted_checks` takes the contract it would be helping to build, and nothing writes a finding today so stage 12 has nothing to compare against. Both are honest records of a real gap rather than a false green, and the gap is what the product's repair/re-check promise (priority 8) is waiting on. Corrected 2026-09-19: this note called P14-T009 "the queued fixture task", and P14-T009 was accepted on 2026-09-19 (head 6f5cc0e3ddcd94621c5540e3673f6a52bb75e65a, finished 07:33:40Z) while this task stayed ready. Its record carries the limit in its own words — "what is NOT claimed. That a process-level `sure check` / `sure repair` / `sure recheck` round trip closes a finding: it does not." This task is what makes that sentence obsolete, so P14-T009's record needs amending when this lands.

title: Bring the corpus's record of detector severity back in line with the detectors
acceptance: Every `detector_severity_today` value in `fixtures/adversarial/*/scenario.json` states what the named detector yields today, measured by running it — or the field is replaced by a statement of where the current value is measured. The historic fact that the required and the delivered severity were once different is not deleted: it lives in `adversarial_fixture_detection.rs`'s `SEVERITY_BEFORE_P7T011` and in git, and this task keeps it.

A test fails when a `detector_severity_today` value disagrees with the severity the detector produces, so the field cannot go stale again. It reads the fixture's own text and runs the detector; a hand-kept list of expected values in the test would be a second place to keep the same fact.

The `notes` sentences that say every detector here emits `Severity::Note`, and that `adversarial_fixture_detection.rs` "pins the gap", are corrected to what the tree now does — that test asserts the manifest's severity now, and says so.

Where a per-outcome `required_severity` cannot be met by the detector that owns the outcome, the corpus says so deliberately: `fake-auth` requires `must_fix` for `CandidateCategory::Todo` at `src/auth.js` while `demo-analytics` requires `should_fix_first` for the same category, in the same context and with the same evidence class, so no function of a proposal's own fields satisfies both. Each such outcome either restates its requirement in terms its detector can meet, or carries the reason it stands unmet and what would have to change for it to be met.

`required_severity` for the release-blocking cases is not lowered to match today's implementation, and `evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json` is unchanged by this task. A corpus edited to agree with the code is the false green this repository exists to catch, one level up.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P7-T011's verification. P7-T011 gave detector findings the severity the corpus required, and in doing so made the corpus's own record of what the detectors do false: `fixtures/adversarial/{fake-payment,fake-auth,fake-email,dead-button,route-mismatch,demo-analytics}/scenario.json` still carry `detector_severity_today: "note"`, and their `notes` sentences still say every detector emits `Severity::Note` and that `adversarial_fixture_detection.rs` pins the gap between that and the requirement. No `.rs` file reads the field, so nothing depended on it — which is exactly why it could go stale unnoticed. The same verification measured the finer statement that remains unmet: in those fixtures the `candidate_scanner` outcomes land at `can_fix_later` while their per-outcome `required_severity` says `must_fix`, and the release-blocking severity arrives through the detector that saw the substituted action itself. `finding_gravity`'s module doc records why the `Todo` case cannot be satisfied by both fixtures at once. P7-T011 deliberately did not edit any of this: the fixtures were off-limits to its worker because a task that measures against a requirement should not be the task that rewrites it afterwards.

title: Let the check report read the capability tier from the project's recorded events
acceptance: `sure check` on a project whose store holds a session's harness events reports the tier those events earn, and with no events it still reports the snapshot tier — both observed by running the command against a project with recorded events and one without, not by a report about them.

The tier comes from `capability_report::report_from_events`, which computes it from the events SURE actually received and refuses a self-reported `Protected` tier; the pipeline does not grow a second rule, and the adapter's own claim is never taken upward.
The blind spots that module already computes are reported beside the tier, so a tier says what it does not cover rather than reading as completeness.
The capability line names what it counted — which harnesses the events came from and over what window — so a reader can tell 'no events were recorded' from 'events exist and were not counted'.

Every document that states a tier claim for a harness (`integrations/*/README.md`, `docs/architecture/MCP_BRIDGE.md`, `docs/architecture/CLI.md`) matches what the report now says, including the case where the events exist but the tier did not rise.
notes: Added 2026-09-18 by the supervisor, from P12-T007's verification. The Codex bridge now reaches Tier 1 on ingest — four events normalised, stored and readable — while `sure check` still prints "capability tier 0, snapshot" for a project that has them, because the pipeline takes the tier from the command line and `crates/sure-core/src/capability_report.rs::report_from_events` has no callers. The same holds for the Claude Code and Cursor bridges (P10-T003, P11-T004), whose accepted work mapped events to a tier the report does not read. This is the safe direction — understating what SURE knows — but it means each integration's tier table promises something the verdict does not deliver, and a reader who records a session and then checks the project is told nothing changed. Related, and separate: `agent.claim` and `user.request` have no production caller, which is why Codex's `Stop` and prompt submissions are refused rather than mapped; giving claims a consumer is its own task and is not required for this one.
